Idée centrale Money received at different dates cannot be compared directly. To compare “apples with apples”, we bring every amount to the same point in time : forward (future value) or backward (present value). 01 Notion Why money has a time value Inflation : in 5 years, the same €100 may buy fewer goods. Investment : €100 today invested 1 year at 10% becomes €110. The extra €10 is the return (here, the interest). Exemple du cours A generous uncle offers €100: today or in 5 years. Most people choose today. Definitions Future value (FV) : the value that a current amount of money will have at a future date after earning interest. Present value (PV) : the value today of an amount of money to be received or paid in the future. With 10%: €100 today → €110 in one year (FV). €100 received in one year is worth \(100/1.10 \approx 90.90\) today (PV). 02 Notion Why interest rates exist Impatience (“myopia”): people prefer to use money today; the future is valued less than the present. Opportunity cost of waiting : a lender who lends €100 cannot use it. The interest compensates this wait (lend €100, get €110 → €10 of interest). Inflation : higher inflation → the lender requires a higher rate. Fisher effect Nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation. Exemple du cours Real return wanted 4%, expected inflation 6% → nominal rate of about 10%. 03 Notion Simple vs compound interest Simple interest Compound interest Interest is… not reinvested (spent) reinvested: interest earns interest €100 at 10%, 3 years €10 per year → €30 of interest in total €110 → €121 → €133.10 Where used specific contexts: trust funds, charitable organizations, university endowments (principal untouched, only the income is spent) the usual way financial markets work Future value (compound) \[ FV = PV \times (1+i)^n \] Example du cours : \( 100 \times 1.10^3 = 133.10 \). The exponent is the number of periods. Present value \[ PV = \dfrac{FV}{(1+i)^n} \] Example du cours : \( 121 / 1.10^2 = 100 \). Banks use present value calculations to set loans: the payments happen in the future, but they must be related to the amount lent today. 04 Méthode Timelines & multiple cash flows Method Draw a timeline (year 0, 1, 2, 3…). Move each cash flow separately to the chosen date (compound it forward or discount it back). Add the results. Exemple du cours — future value €100 today and €100 in year 1, rate 10%, value in year 2: \(100\times1.10^2 = 121\) and \(100\times1.10 = 110\) → €231 . The interest earned on the first €100 is reinvested (compound interest). The second €100 earns interest for one year only. Exemple du cours — present value €100 in year 1 and €100 in year 2, rate 10%: \(100/1.10 = 90.90\) and \(100/1.10^2 = 82.64\) → €173.54 . With €173.54 invested at 10% today, you can pay €100 in year 1 and €100 in year 2. The amounts don’t have to be equal (€60, €42, €100…). Each has a different value depending on when it is received: this is the common reference point for CFOs and finance teams evaluating projects. 05 Notion Annuities Annuity Equal (constant) cash flows at regular intervals. Most loans are annuities: mortgage loans, business loans, many standard bank loans. Notation in the course: A (or a ) = regular payment, i = interest rate, n = number of periods. Spreadsheet names: PVA (present value of an annuity), FVA (future value of an annuity), PMT (payment). Unknown Given Excel (French version) PV (lump sum) FV, i, n VA FV (lump sum) PV, i, n VC PVA a, i, n VA FVA a, i, n VC PMT (from a loan amount PVA) PVA, i, n VPM PMT (to reach a target FVA) FVA, i, n VPM Information absente des notes The PV-of-an-annuity formula itself is not written in the text of the notes (the professor says it is more important to understand than to memorize it). The logic is: PVA = sum of the present values of each payment. The spreadsheet exercises use the Excel functions above. Computation check below uses that logic. Understanding rule (professor): understand how it works and what each element represents ; experiment in Excel by changing payment, rate or periods. 06 Distinction APR vs EAR APR (annual percentage rate) EAR (effective annual rate) What it is Annual rate used to derive the periodic rate . Information in the loan contract, not the rate you really pay. The rate you actually pay per year , once compounding is taken into account. Link Periodic rate = APR / number of periods (monthly: APR/12 ; daily: APR/365) Compound the periodic rate over the periods of one year, then subtract the €1 borrowed Size Smaller Bigger (the gap can be significant) In France Taux débiteur annuel — both must be declared, but the APR is the one most cited because it is smaller TAEG (taux annuel effectif global) — lets you compare offers Conversions (course method) \[ APR = \text{periodic rate} \times \text{number of periods per year} \] \[ EAR = (1+\text{periodic rate})^{m} - 1 \quad (m = \text{periods per year}) \] EAR method of the professor: borrow €1 for the 12 months (or 365 days) at the periodic rate, compute the future value (compounding), subtract the €1 borrowed. Exemple du cours Credit card with a daily rate of 0.05% : APR = 0.05% × 365 = 18.25% . In the US, card rates above 15% a year were common; a card announcing “15% APR” may really cost about 17% (“a couple of percentage points more”). Pièges The APR is not what you pay. When a problem gives an APR with monthly payments, use APR/12 as the periodic rate and years × 12 as n. Incohérence dans les documents The “EAR” spreadsheet shows a periodic rate of 0.1% but its statement says 0.05% daily. The expected answer is therefore unclear. Computed with the statement (0.05%): EAR = 1.0005 365 − 1 ≈ 20.02% . With 0.1% it would be ≈ 44.03%. The lecture transcript is also partly garbled on this topic; only the clear parts are kept here. 07 Application Amortization schedule Method (for each year / period) PMT from the loan amount (PVA), the rate and n (Excel VPM). Interest paid = beginning balance × rate. Principal paid = payment − interest paid. Ending balance = beginning balance − principal paid (= next period’s beginning balance). Last ending balance = 0. Exercices d’entraînement Exercice d’entraînement généré A — Four criteria on one project Investment 1,200 at t=0; CFs: 300, 400, 500, 600 (years 1–4). Required return 8%. Compute NPV, IRR, PI, payback and discounted payback. Voir la correction NPV = 300/1.08 + 400/1.08² + 500/1.08³ + 600/1.08⁴ − 1,200. PVs: 277.78 ; 342.94 ; 396.92 ; 441.02 → sum 1,458.65 → NPV ≈ 258.65 > 0. IRR (Excel, range incl. t=0) ≈ 16.28% > 8% → accept. PI = 1 + 258.65/1,200 ≈ 1.22 > 1 → accept. Payback : cumulative CFs 300, 700, 1,200 → recovered exactly at the end of year 3 → 3.0 years . Idée centrale Capital budgeting = decision process corporations use when they invest capital in new ventures: the comparison of costs versus future profits (advertising campaign, R&D, acquiring a competitor…). 01 Méthode Criteria & standard steps Criteria most often used: NPV , IRR , Profitability Index (PI) , Payback Period (“not so good”), Discounted Payback Period . Standard steps Estimate CFs (inflows & outflows). Assess riskiness of CFs. Determine the cost of capital i for the project. Find NPV and/or IRR and/or PI. Accept if NPV > 0 and/or IRR > WACC and/or PI > 1 . 02 Critère Net Present Value (NPV) Definition NPV = Present Value minus the monetary value of the initial investment (“Net” because the initial investment is taken into account). For a project: the value of the income generated in excess of the initial investment (cost of the project). The discount rate i is generally the cost of capital appropriate for the company and its project. Formula \[ NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t} + CF_0 \] \(i\) = discount rate · \(CF_t\) = cash flow at time t · \(CF_0\) = initial investment (usually a negative number) NPV = PV inflows − PV of cost = net gain in wealth. Decision rule NPV > 0 : PV of the income stream is greater than the cost → accept (above-normal profits). NPV < 0 : cost is greater than the income stream → reject . Properties: the most used criterion · considers the time value of money · absolute measure of wealth (positive NPVs increase the owner’s wealth, negative ones decrease it) · discount rate = cost of capital · project CFs are assumed reinvested at the cost of capital. How a firm can generate above-normal profits: buyers’ preference for established brand names · control of distribution systems · patent control · exclusive ownership of superior natural resources · access to lower-cost financial resources · economies of scale · access to superior labor or management talents. Exemple du cours — Project A, WACC = 10% CFs: −100 (t=0), 10, 60, 80. PVs: 9.09 + 49.59 + 60.11 = 118.79 (rounded), so NPV A ≈ 18.79 → positive → accept. (Unrounded: 18.78.) Excel trap (from the exercises’ tip) NPV(rate, range) discounts the first value by one period. So write =NPV(rate, CF1:CFn)+CF0 . IRR needs the full range including time 0 . 03 Notion NPV and the discount rate The higher the discount rate, the smaller the NPV (everything else equal); the smaller the rate, the larger the NPV. Exemple du cours — PV of a CF of 10 at t=1 Rate PV 1% 10/1.01 = 9.90 10% 10/1.10 = 9.09 20% 10/1.20 = 8.33 Reading the NPV-vs-rate graph (rate on x-axis, NPV on y-axis): the curve falls as the rate rises; there is a rate where NPV = 0, and beyond it NPV is negative. In the course graph, NPV reaches 0 at almost 17%, and the NPV at 4% is 21.83 (cash flows of that Excel application are not shown in the notes). 04 Critère Internal Rate of Return (IRR) Definition The IRR is the rate at which the NPV is zero : the break-even point (expected cash flows cover exactly the cost of the project, considering the time value of money). Formula \[ NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+IRR)^t} = 0 \] Excel: IRR (French version: TRI). Decision rule Accept if IRR > discount rate (also called required return, cost of capital or “hurdle rate”). Intuition: the expected return exceeds the required rate of return. In investment projects we speak of required return to stress that investors demand it (chapter 5, WACC). IRR usually gives the same decision as NPV. Limit: for purely algebraic reasons, solving for the IRR may lead to several solutions. Conclusion of the course: it is better to use the NPV rule. Exemple du cours — office building (foregone opportunity 14%) Cost \(C_0\) = $370m; sale in year 1 \(C_1\) = $420m. Return = (420,000 − 370,000)/370,000 = 0.135 = 13.5% . It is below 14%, so by the IRR rule the project is not accepted (the notes show the computation, not the written verdict). Exemple du cours — investment project NPV = 52.07 (positive → accept). IRR = 9.49% > 7% required → green-lighted: the project gives more income than its cost. The NPV graph shows NPV > 0 for rates below 9.49% (project accepted) and NPV < 0 above (rejected). The cash flows of this example are in an embedded Excel not reproduced in the notes. Exemple du cours — Projects S and L (cost of capital 14%) t 0 1 2 3 4 IRR S −1,000 500 400 300 100 14.49% L −1,000 100 300 400 675 13.55% S: IRR 14.49% > 14% → accept. L: IRR 13.55% < 14% → reject. Écart dans le document The course sheet shows NPV S = 7.09 and NPV L = −10.35. Recomputed with the standard formula at 14%: NPV S = 8.08 and NPV L = −11.80 . The sheet’s values equal these divided by 1.14: they correspond to the Excel trap above (NPV function applied to the range including t=0). Signs and decisions are unchanged. 05 Critère Profitability Index (PI) Formula \[ PI = 1 + \frac{NPV}{\text{Investment}} \] Accept a project if PI > 1 ; do not accept if PI < 1. When resources are limited , PI helps select among project combinations: the highest weighted average PI indicates which projects to select. Exemple du cours — three projects Project C0 C1 C2 NPV @10% Investment PI A −10 +30 +5 21 10 3.1 B −5 +5 +20 16 5 4.2 C −5 +5 +15 12 5 3.4 Ex: PI(A) = 1 + 21/10 = 3.1 ($ millions). (Even though A has the highest individual PI.) 06 Critère Payback & discounted payback Payback period The number of years required to recover a project’s cost: how long does it take to get the business’s money back? Computation Payback = last full period where accumulated cash flows are still below the initial investment + last (partial) period. Partial period = (remainder still to recover) / (next cash flow). Remarque The notes word the partial period as “next cash flow / remainder”, but all their examples compute remainder ÷ next cash flow (30/80, 30/50). Use the examples’ version. Exemple du cours — Project B (CFs mostly in later years) CFs: −100, 10, 60, 80 · cumulative: −100, −90, −30, +50 → payback = 2 + 30/80 = 2.375 years (shown as 2.4). Exemple du cours — Project C (CFs come quickly) CFs: −100, 70, 50, 20 · cumulative: −100, −30, +20, +40 → payback = 1 + 30/50 = 1.6 years . Strengths Weaknesses Gives an indication of a project’s risk and liquidity ; easy to calculate and understand Ignores the time value of money ; ignores CFs occurring after the payback period Discounted payback Same method but with discounted rather than raw CFs. Exemple du cours — Project A at 10% CFs −100, 10, 60, 80 → PV: −100, 9.09, 49.59, 60.11 · cumulative: −100, −90.91, −41.32, +18.79 → discounted payback = 2 + 41.32/60.11 = 2.7 years . Reading: investment and capital costs recovered in 2.7 years. 07 Comparaison Which criterion says what? Criterion Accept if Uses TVM? Interprétation : NPV > 0 and IRR (23.3%) > 15% required return → invest . Exercice d’entraînement généré B — Selling an old asset (replacement) An old machine has a book value of $10,000. It can be sold for (a) $6,000 or (b) $13,000. Tax rate 34%. What is the cash flow from the sale in each case? Voir la correction (a) Selling price < book value : tax concession = (10,000 − 6,000) × 34% = 1,360; CF = 6,000 + 1,360 = $7,360 . (b) Selling price > book value : tax = (13,000 − 10,000) × 34% = 1,020; CF = 13,000 − 1,020 = $11,980 . Interprétation : selling at a loss gives a tax saving (more cash than the price); selling at a gain triggers a tax (less cash than the price). Exercice d’entraînement généré C — From OCF to free cash flow A firm has OCF = 500, capital expenditures = 120 and a change in net working capital of 30. Compute the free cash flow. Then compute it again if net working capital falls by 30 instead. Voir la correction Formule : FCF = OCF − Capex − ΔNWC. Case 1 (ΔNWC = +30): FCF = 500 − 120 − 30 = 350 . Case 2 (ΔNWC = −30): FCF = 500 − 120 − (−30) = 410 . Interprétation : an increase in working capital uses cash; a decrease releases it. Compute CFO. Voir la correction Formule du cours : CFO = Net income + Depreciation − Non-op. gains + Non-op. losses − ΔOperating assets + ΔOperating liabilities. CFO = 80 + 30 − 5 − 12 + 4 = 97 . Interprétation : the gain on land is non-operating (removed), the increase in receivables/inventory absorbs cash, the increase in payables brings cash.

Idée centrale Determining cash flows is “the most important and difficult task in capital budgeting” . Only incremental, after-tax cash flows matter — not accounting profit. OCF = EBIT − Taxes + Depreciation and FCF = OCF − Capex − ΔNWC . 01 Révision The statement of cash flows Net income mixes accrual revenues and expenses, so it rarely equals the cash generated. The cash flow statement reclassifies every cash movement into three buckets: Bucket Content Meaning Operating (CFO) Collections from customers · payments to suppliers & employees · interest paid/received, taxes paid The engine of the business — day-to-day cash generation Investing (CFI) Purchases of PP&E / capex · sales of PP&E or land · purchases & sales of financial investments Building (or shrinking) the firm’s productive capacity Financing (CFF) New borrowings & loan repayments · share issuance & buybacks · dividends paid How the firm is funded — debt, equity, and payouts Direct vs indirect method — same answer, two routes Direct : lists actual cash receipts and payments (needs access to the cash account). Optional under IFRS / US GAAP, but firms using it must still disclose the indirect reconciliation. Indirect : starts from net income and adjusts for non-cash items — presented in the course as the mandatory presentation under IFRS & US GAAP. Indirect method CFO = Net income + Depreciation − Non-op. gains + Non-op. losses − ΔOperating assets + ΔOperating liabilities Exemple du cours (fictitious) — both methods give CFO = 93 Direct Indirect Collections from customers +1,191 Net income 55 Payments to suppliers −782 + Depreciation (non-cash) +54 Payments to employees −280 − Gain on land sale (non-operating) −4 Interest & taxes paid −36 − Δ Accounts receivable / inventory −15 CFO 93 + Δ Payables (A/P, interest payable) +3 CFO 93 Exemple du cours — Adobe Inc., FY2025 (10-K, $ millions) Item $M Net income 7,130 Depreciation & other non-cash items 2,296 Change in working capital 605 CFO 10,031 Capital expenditures −179 Acquisitions, net of investment sales/purchases −1,008 CFI −1,187 Share repurchases −11,281 Share issuance & net debt activity +845 Other financing activities −624 CFF −11,060 Cash bridge: beginning cash $7,613M + CFO 10,031 + CFI (−1,187) + CFF (−11,060) + FX effect 34 = ending cash $5,431M (net change −2,182). Despite $10.0B of operating cash flow, cash fell — driven by $11.3B of share repurchases, the largest use of cash. Free cash flow FY2025 = CFO 10,031 − Capex 179 = $9,852M . Capex is only ~2% of CFO in FY2025 vs ~5% in FY2021 (asset-light subscription software model). CFO up 39% since FY2021; CFF consistently negative (buybacks dominate). 02 Formules Operating cash flow & free cash flow OCF (project-level formula) \[ OCF = EBIT - Taxes + Depreciation \] Start from operating profit, remove cash taxes, add back the non-cash depreciation charge. FCF (firm-level formula) = Cash flow from assets \[ FCF = OCF - Capex - \Delta NWC \] Cash left after reinvesting in fixed assets and working capital — available to repay debt and reward shareholders. (In the notes: “change in net operating working capital”.) The same logic used to evaluate a single project scales up to a whole company. 03 Principes Project evaluation: which cash flows count? Definitions Project evaluation : applying one or more capital budgeting decision rules to the estimated relevant project cash flows to make the investment decision. Relevant cash flows : the incremental cash flows associated with the decision to invest in a project — any and all changes in the firm’s future cash flows that are a direct consequence of taking the project. Stand-alone principle : evaluating a project based on its incremental cash flows; view each project as a “mini-firm” with its own assets, revenues and costs. If projects interact, they can be bunched together. Issue Rule Only cash flow Estimate on an incremental basis (how the project changes the firm’s cash flows — especially relevant to depreciation); always after tax Sunk costs Do not include : past, irreversible outflows, not affected by the accept/reject decision Opportunity costs Include Side effects Include all incidental effects Net working capital Include : new projects often require cash, inventories and receivables; often recovered when the project ends Financing costs Not counted (interest, principal on debt, dividends): the discount rate takes care of them Key issues listed: when is a cash flow incremental · terminology: A. sunk costs, B. opportunity costs, C. side effects, D. net working capital, E. financing costs, F. other issues. Capital expenditure decisions listed: expand an existing product line · working capital · refunding · leasing · merger and acquisition · enter a new line of business · replacement · advertising campaign · R&D · education and training. 04 Méthode Specific rules for cash flow accounting 1. Initial outlay (−) Cost of the asset (installed) (−) Additional working capital investments (+) Cash flow from sale of an old asset (replacement situation): Selling price > book value: tax = (selling price − book value) × tax rate; CF = selling price − tax Selling price < book value: tax concession = (book value − selling price) × tax rate; CF = selling price + tax concession 2. Intermediate cash flows (operations) (+) Added revenues · (−) increased expenses, including overhead · (+) savings: labor and material (+) Depreciation expense (add back) Do not include interest expense. 3. Terminal cash flow (closing the business) (+) Sale of fixed assets (after the tax effect above) (+) Recapture of working capital Depreciation Straight line : a fixed percentage of the asset base.
